blocks.x: The question is not whether to fine-tune but who owns the resulting model risk.
Fine-tuning is a governance decision, not a modeling one. Curated corpora beat corpus size; licensing and PII posture decide auditability.
LoRA/QLoRA economics make iteration weekly — if the registry and eval gates exist.
EU AI Act technical documentation is cheapest when generated during training, not after.

Applied carelessly, it breaks the same way every time — retrieval appended after the model choice, permissions mapped after launch, freshness treated as an ops afterthought — each producing the same symptom: answers nobody defends when the audit arrives.

The strongest counter-case, stated fairly: the retrieval-first thesis can excuse weak models. It should not: retrieval multiplies whatever the model does, so evaluation stays the arbiter in both directions.
The practice, as we run it

In delivery, this thesis becomes a specific discipline: the work is model and retrieval engineering with evaluation wired in from the first sprint — grounded answers, cited sources, and a cost line somebody actually owns. Every program in the Applied AI & GenAI domain carries the same obligations — a signed baseline, named gate criteria, and evidence generated by running the system rather than preparing for a meeting.
The next step is small and real: one working session on fine-tuning is a governance decision, not a modeling one, your data, and a written feasibility read you can circulate.
